title: What is the difference between `git merge`, `git rebase`, and `git cherry-pick`, and when do you use each?
shortTitle: The difference between git merge, git rebase, and git cherry-pick, and when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: `git merge` combines two branches by creating a merge commit that has both branch tips as parents, preserving the true history of parallel development. `git rebase` moves or replays the commits of one branch onto the tip of another, rewriting those commits as new commits to produce a linear history as if the work had been done sequentially. `git cherry-pick` copies one or more specific commits from anywhere and applies them as new commits onto the current branch, without bringing the rest of the source branch. Merge preserves history and is safe on shared branches; rebase rewrites history and so is used on local or private branches to keep history clean; cherry-pick selectively transplants individual commits.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture how the National Bank of India records work. Merge is like stapling two teams' separate logbooks together with a cover note saying "these two streams of work joined here" — the true, honest record of parallel effort is kept. Rebase is like one team rewriting their logbook so it reads as if their work was done neatly after the other team's, producing one clean straight story — tidier to read, but it is a rewritten record, so you only do it before anyone else has copied it. Cherry-pick is like taking one single important page out of one logbook — say the fix that corrected Rajesh's fee — and copying just that page into another logbook, without bringing the whole book.
s1_definition.oneliner: Merge joins branches and keeps true history, rebase replays commits for a clean linear history but rewrites them, and cherry-pick copies specific individual commits — use merge on shared branches, rebase on private ones, cherry-pick to transplant a single fix.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `git merge` combines two branches by creating a merge commit that has both branch tips as parents, preserving the true history of parallel development. `git rebase` moves or replays the commits of one branch onto the tip of another, rewriting those commits as new commits to produce a linear history as if the work had been done sequentially. `git cherry-pick` copies one or more specific commits from anywhere and applies them as new commits onto the current branch, without bringing the rest of the source branch. Merge preserves history and is safe on shared branches; rebase rewrites history and so is used on local or private branches to keep history clean; cherry-pick selectively transplants individual commits.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture how the National Bank of India records work. Merge is like stapling two teams' separate logbooks together with a cover note saying "these two streams of work joined here" — the true, honest record of parallel effort is kept. Rebase is like one team rewriting their logbook so it reads as if their work was done neatly after the other team's, producing one clean straight story — tidier to read, but it is a rewritten record, so you only do it before anyone else has copied it. Cherry-pick is like taking one single important page out of one logbook — say the fix that corrected Rajesh's fee — and copying just that page into another logbook, without bringing the whole book.

**One line to remember:** Merge joins branches and keeps true history, rebase replays commits for a clean linear history but rewrites them, and cherry-pick copies specific individual commits — use merge on shared branches, rebase on private ones, cherry-pick to transplant a single fix.

sections.s2_technical:
Merge integrates one branch into another by creating a new merge commit with two parents, one pointing to each branch's previous tip. This records the fact that development happened in parallel and then came together. Merge never changes existing commits; it only adds the merge commit, so it is non-destructive and completely safe to use on shared branches that others have pulled. The cost is that the history graph has branches and merge commits, which some people find noisier to read, especially with many feature branches. A special case is a fast-forward merge: if the target branch has not moved since the feature branched, Git can simply move the pointer forward without a merge commit, giving a linear result; teams often force a merge commit with `--no-ff` to keep a visible record of each feature.

Rebase takes the commits that are unique to your branch and replays them one by one onto the tip of another branch, creating new commits with new hashes that have the same changes but new parentage. The result is a straight, linear history with no merge commits, as though you had started your work from the latest base. Interactive rebase, `git rebase -i`, additionally lets you reorder, squash, edit, or drop your commits before replaying, which is excellent for cleaning up a messy feature branch into a few logical commits before review. The critical caveat is that because rebase creates new commits and abandons the old ones, it rewrites history, so you must never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch and pulled by others, for exactly the same reason you never reset-and-force-push shared history — everyone else would diverge. Rebase is therefore a tool for your own local or private branches: you rebase your feature branch onto the latest main to keep it current and to resolve conflicts incrementally before merging.

Cherry-pick copies specific commits by their hash and applies their changes as brand new commits on your current branch. It does not bring along the rest of the source branch's history, just the chosen commits. This is surgical: you reach into one branch, take exactly the commit or commits you want, and apply them elsewhere. Because the applied commit is a new commit with a new hash, cherry-pick also technically creates new history, but it is additive on the target, so it is safe in the sense of not rewriting the target's existing commits.

Choosing between them comes down to intent. You use merge to integrate a completed feature into a shared branch while preserving the honest record, and it is the default safe choice for anything others depend on. You use rebase to keep a private feature branch up to date with main and to tidy its commits into a clean, linear story before it is merged, giving a readable history — a common team policy is "rebase your feature branch locally, then merge it with a merge commit." You use cherry-pick when you need a specific change somewhere without the rest of its branch: the classic case is a hotfix made on a release branch that you want to also apply to main, or backporting one bug fix to an older supported version. A senior nuance: many teams adopt a hybrid policy — rebase locally to keep history clean and linear, but merge to shared branches so no shared history is ever rewritten — which captures the readability of rebase with the safety of merge. And you avoid cherry-pick as a routine integration mechanism because it duplicates commits, which can cause confusing double-applies and conflicts when the branches are later merged; it is a targeted tool, not a substitute for merging.
sections.s3_banking:
A developer at the National Bank of India is working on a feature branch for the transfer service while main advances, and separately a hotfix is made on a release branch that must also reach main.

Problem 1 — The feature branch has fallen behind main. The developer rebases the private feature branch onto the latest main to keep it current and produce a clean linear history before review, which is safe because the feature branch is private.

Problem 2 — The completed feature is integrated into the shared main branch with a merge, creating a merge commit that honestly records the parallel work and never rewrites shared history.

Problem 3 — A critical fee-rounding hotfix was committed on the release branch for Rajesh's and Priya's transfers. It must also be applied to main without dragging the rest of the release branch. The developer cherry-picks just that one commit onto main.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `Branch` of commits and a `GitOps` engine with `rebase`, `merge`, and `cherryPick`, logging how each operation reshapes history. Classes: `Commit`, `Branch`, `GitOps`, and a `MergeRebaseCherryDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.vcs.MergeRebaseCherryDemo

# Real commands:
# Rebase a PRIVATE feature branch onto latest main (clean, linear):
git checkout feature/instant-transfer
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main        # replay my commits onto main
git rebase -i origin/main                          # also squash/reorder before review

# Merge the feature into shared main (preserve history, never rewrite shared):
git checkout main && git merge --no-ff feature/instant-transfer

# Cherry-pick ONE hotfix commit from a release branch onto main:
git checkout main && git cherry-pick <hotfix-sha>
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a shared main branch that has advanced to two commits, a private feature branch that was cut earlier and now trails main, and a release branch carrying a single hotfix commit.

Step 1: The feature branch is private, so the rebase is allowed. The engine replays the feature's unique commit — the instant-transfer work — on top of the latest main, creating a new commit with a new id. The feature branch now reads as a clean linear history starting from the current main, with no merge commits, exactly as if the work had begun from today's main.

Step 2: The completed feature is merged into the shared main branch. The merge brings the feature's commit into main and adds a merge commit with both tips as parents. This honestly records that the feature was developed in parallel and then integrated, and because merge only adds commits, it never rewrites the shared main history that others have pulled.

Step 3: A release branch separately contains a critical fee-rounding hotfix for transfers involving Rajesh and Priya. This fix is needed on main too, but the rest of the release branch is not.

Step 4: The engine cherry-picks only the hotfix commit onto main, copying its change as a new commit without bringing any other release-branch history. Main now has the hotfix applied surgically.

Step 5: Across the three operations the distinct purposes are clear: rebase produced a clean linear private history, merge integrated into shared history while preserving the true record, and cherry-pick transplanted exactly one needed commit. Each tool matched a different intent.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The three operations differ in how they reshape history. Git merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit that has both branch tips as parents, which honestly records that development happened in parallel and then came together. Merge never changes existing commits — it only adds the merge commit — so it is non-destructive and completely safe on shared branches that others have pulled. The trade-off is a history graph with branches and merge commits, which some find noisier.

Git rebase takes the commits unique to my branch and replays them one by one onto the tip of another branch, creating new commits with new hashes that carry the same changes but new parentage, producing a straight, linear history as though I had started from the latest base. Interactive rebase also lets me squash, reorder, and clean up my commits before review. The crucial caveat is that because rebase creates new commits and abandons the old ones, it rewrites history, so I never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch and pulled by others — that would make everyone diverge. Rebase is a tool for my own private branches. Git cherry-pick copies specific commits by their hash and applies their changes as new commits on my current branch, without bringing the rest of the source branch — it is surgical, reaching in to take exactly the commit I want.

Choosing between them is about intent. I use merge to integrate a completed feature into a shared branch while preserving the true record, and it is the default safe choice for anything others depend on. I use rebase to keep a private feature branch current with main and to tidy its commits into a clean linear story before merging. I use cherry-pick when I need one specific change somewhere without the rest of its branch, the classic case being a hotfix made on a release branch that must also reach main, or backporting a single fix to an older version. In my project at the National Bank of India, I would rebase my private instant-transfer feature onto the latest main for a clean linear history, then merge it into shared main with a merge commit so no shared history was ever rewritten, and when a fee-rounding hotfix for transfers involving Rajesh and Priya landed on a release branch, I cherry-picked just that one commit onto main rather than dragging the whole branch. The policy I always state is rebase private branches for clean history, merge to shared branches so shared history is never rewritten, and cherry-pick for a targeted fix or backport — and I avoid cherry-pick as a routine integration mechanism because duplicating commits causes confusing double-applies when branches are later merged.
